      37             : // Note [Python interpreter tag]
      38             : // ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
      39             : // Traditionally, PyTorch is layered such that our Python library
      40             : // (libtorch_python) references our pure C++ library (libtorch) as the
      41             : // natural order of things.  However, sometimes this natural order is
      42             : // subverted: C++ objects refer to Python objects (for example, we
      43             : // store a PyObject* pointer on TensorImpl so that converting from a
      44             : // C++ Tensor to a Python Tensor is just a memory dereference).
      45             : //
      46             : // These unusual orderings must be treated with care.  To start, you need to
      47             : // virtualize the destructor so that the PyObject can be decref'ed on
      48             : // destruction (because the C++ object itself doesn't know anything about
      49             : // Python--remember, layering!).  This process itself is fraught, since
      50             : // acquiring the GIL could lead to deadlocks if someone is blocking on you
      51             : // while holding the GIL.  Furthermore, if the C++ objects outlive the
      52             : // interpreter (which can happen if you stash them in a static global
      53             : // variable defined in libtorch), you may attempt to decref the object when
      54             : // the Python interpreter has already been shutdown.
      55             : //
      56             : // BUT WAIT, IT GETS WORSE.  With torchdeploy, there may be multiple Python
      57             : // interpreters in a single process. If a C++ object is accessible from
      58             : // multiple interpreters, we must take care not to accidentally pass a
      59             : // PyObject from one interpreter with another interpreter.
      60             : //
      61             : // To prevent these mixups, we introduce a PyInterpreter "tag" (object with
      62             : // a vtable), which specifies a specific Python interpreter.
      63             : //
      64             : //  - Any given object can be associated with AT MOST one Python interpreter.
      65             : //    We represent the interpreter tag as a memory address to an instance of
      66             : //    a virtual class that is allocated once per interpreter (this is so that
      67             : //    we can request the interpreter to perform operations for us, if
      68             : //    necessary).
      69             : //
      70             : //  - It can be recorded with a PyObject (PyInterpreterObject) so that
      71             : //    we know what interpreter the object is associated with, and we can
      72             : //    raise an error if you try to use the PyObject from the wrong
      73             : //    interpreter context.
      74             : //
      75             : //  - It contains a vtable that can be used to perform various Python
      76             : //    operations from ordinary C++ code that ordinarily wouldn't be accessible
      77             : //    from libtorch.
      78             : //
      79             : // A simple use case is when a C++ object must be associated with a PyObject.
      80             : // However, for TensorImpl, we lazily allocate a PyObject the first time the
      81             : // object passes into Python.  The invariants for this situation are more
      82             : // subtle:
      83             : //
      84             : //  - A given TensorImpl's interpreter tag can only go from uninitialized to
      85             : //    tagged; once tagged, this is a quiescent state (once tagged to an
      86             : //    interpreter, ALWAYS tagged to that interpreter)
      87             : //
      88             : //  - A thread may mutate the PyObject field of a TensorImpl if and only if it
      89             : //    holds the GIL for the interpreter tagged on the TensorImpl.  (If the
      90             : //    TensorImpl is not tagged, it must first atomically claim its tag before it
      91             : //    can validly write)
      92             : //
      93             : // WARNING: This class has to be written very carefully, because it may be
      94             : // possible for a Tensor to have a reference an interpreter corresponding to
      95             : // a shared library that has ALREADY BEEN UNLOADED.  This makes blindly calling
      96             : // virtual methods very dangerous, because the vtable may be garbage at that
      97             : // point (on a good day, you might get "pure virtual method called").
      98             : //
      99             : // The idea to solve this problem is we always leak PyInterpreters (so they
     100             : // always stay live even after dlclose), and make sure we can disarm their
     101             : // virtual methods by indirecting through a separate PyInterpreterVTable
     102             : // object.  This can be replaced with a no-op vtable from libc10.so, which
     103             : // is guaranteed to stick around until the bitter end.
     104             : //
     105             : // NB: The downside with representing PyInterpreter tags as full objects is that
     106             : // it takes an extra word on TensorImpl.  If tags were instead just integer
     107             : // indices, on 64-bit architectures we could pack the tag and PyObject together
     108             : // into a single atomic word.  On 32-bit architectures we could simply say that
     109             : // only one Python interpreter is supported (erroring if a nontrivial
     110             : // interpreter tag is attempted to be set).
     111             : //
     112             : // The difficulty with this scheme is we need to maintain an out-of-line table
     113             : // to get at the PyInterpreters so that we can do virtual method calls on them,
     114             : // and registration/deregistration to this table must be done in a thread safe
     115             : // manner.  This can be easily done if the number of possible PyInterpreters is
     116             : // small enough (e.g., 8-bit integer) by simply preallocating an array of
     117             : // sufficient size to hold all possible interpreters.  Surely 128 threads is
     118             : // more than enough for anyone!
     119             : //
     120             : // I didn't decide to do this technique at the moment, because the extra word
     121             : // added by the PyInterpreter tag takes us to 24 words, which means that we
     122             : // still fit inside three eight word cache lines.  If you need to penny pinch
     123             : // another word consider doing this!
